questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose McGill University both for its strong science profile and general academic level. For me, it was important to visit a university that had an academic level at least as high as UCPH. I used a lot of time (before choosing the university) to look into what possible courses I would be able to follow. Furthermore, Montreal seemed like a great city to live and study in, both because of its culture and young and vibrant atmosphere.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Surprisingly, neither visa and study permit were acquired to study in Montreal for less than 6 months - this took some time to figure out. McGill's website is not the most intuitive, but with a bit of patience all informations was possible to dig up. Several zoom meeting were available to guide us with everything associated with the arrival and course registration, which was very helpfull.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: At the airport, volunteers were there to help with any questions to incoming exchange students. How to get to downtown Montreal, etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I was in contact with the exchange student advisors at McGill a couple of times, and they were happy to help with any questions.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I ended up living at a student residence off campus - this was pretty easy to find since I found it and signed the lease 4 months before arrival. The lease was quite expensive, however, I lived downtown-downtown with just 5 min. walk to campus. However, I would not recommend living at these student housing off campus since most of them only do leases for 8 or 12 months. I therefore had to find a person to take over my lease, and this took me quite some time, and was a bit stressfull. I lived at LaMARQ and have both good and less good things to say about it (I was a bit unlucky with my flat mates, so this also have a say in my overall experience of LaMARQ, unfortunately).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Montreal. There are many Facebook groups where it is possible to find a room. And they are up to 40% less expensive than what I ended up paying.
I would recommend living downtown or at the part of the plateau that is closest to campus/downtown. In the winter it is nice to be close to downtown.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration itself was easy, however, there are so many courses that it can be kind of a jungle to search through. Expect to use som time on this. The course description is not as thorough as I'm used to at UCPH.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A course schedule app was available to help visualize when each course had lectures, to make sure they didn't overlap. This was very helpfull.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Since being a master student, I was looking for courses with a level above 300. It turned out that some courses were not available for exchange studentes, other not available to students at specific faculties. So I didn't find that many very interesting courses, compared to what was available at UCPH. But I got all the courses I ended up wanting to take.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember to register as soon as the registration opens to make sure to get the spots. Registration opens to different groups of students at different times.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had one 300-level course and three 500-level courses. As a master student I think the course level were sufficient (being close to finish my degree, I wanted to take with a certain academic level), however, the work load was also quite high in the last half of the semester. As a bachelor student, I would recommend 0 or 1 course at 500, to make sure to have time also to explore Montreal and Canada.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I didn't experience any group work, but rather more ‘static teaching' (lectures). I prefer the teaching style at UCPH, but in general it was ok.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ANAT 365 - Cellular Trafficking
BMDE 507 - Formulation & Delivery of Biotherapeutics
PHGY 518 - Artificial Cells
PHGY 520 - Ion Channels

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend BMDE 507. The working load was sufficient, with both lectures, presentations, and assignments. The material was interesting and very relevant (a lot of new research and drugs/products). 
I found PHGY 520 quite difficult because I didn't have sufficient prerequisite. PHGY 518 was chill, but I didn't learn much new stuff, mostly because it was unstructured and consisted of a lot of student presentations. ANAT 365 was ok, but the midterm and final exam was extremely difficult.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I found fresh produce (fruit, veggies, meat) quite expensive. The plane ticket home was very expensive, because I bought it 1-2 months before leaving. So when you buy the ticket to go there, make sure also to buy the return ticket that can be changed - this is much cheaper!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I was really surprised at how many clubs there was available (sports, cultural, etc.). And the people there are really open to new members!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I joined the outdoors club (MOC). I attended very few of the events, which I regret, because they seem really nice.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I took weekend trips to Quebec City and a roadtrip around Ottawa. Quebec City is nice to visit just for a day or two. Then I rented a caravan with a friend and went on a “roadtrip” around Ottawa in the autumn where we visited national parks - this might be the best experience on my whole exchange stay, and was really beautiful with all the fall colors on the trees. I also went on a couple on hiking trips around Montreal, and wish I would have done more since the nature is amazing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found the Canadians really open and welcoming. So despite the culture being half francophone, it was really easy to adapt. I found the culture very similar to the one in Copenhagen.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a couple of clubs at the university (especially MOC) and be open to go on hiking trips etc. with people you haven't met yet.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I went to a couple of ‘local' private house parties, and found the drinking culture less heavy, which was nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Don't join the faculty Froshes! A lot of very young people join these (down to 17 years of age) and they basically just drink in one week. I joined one of the outdoor froshes (the canoeing frosh) and this was really nice + I got an unforgettable trip in a natural park. 2) If you like to hike and spend time in the nature, make sure to bring hiking boots and warm clothes so you can also enjoy the nature in the cold months. 3) Make sure to explore the city and go on weekend trips from the beginning of your stay. Soon, it will be exam period and you will have missed important experiences, which you will regret.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Pack less clothes that you think. You don't need 7 knitted sweaters and 7 pairs of pants (as I brought) - leave some space in your luggage to buy stuff over there.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting a lot of new people, trying another studying culture, and explore Canada's nature.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I found the work load of the courses extremely high during last 1,5 months of my stay (while it was very small the first couple of months). So make sure to make your assignments early in the semester.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
